## Proof

Let $\sigma \in \Sigma$ have $n$ vertices, and enumerate them as $\sigma = \{v_1, \dots, v_n\}$. Define the **open $(n-1)$-simplex**

$$\Delta^{\circ}_{n-1} = \Big\{(x_1,\dots,x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n \;\Big|\; x_i > 0 \text{ for all } i,\; \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i = 1\Big\},$$

equipped with the subspace topology from $\mathbb{R}^n$. Its dimension is $n - 1 = |\sigma| - 1$, as required.

We give $S(V,\Sigma)$ the subspace topology inherited from $[0,1]^V$ (product topology), and hence the subset

$$S_\sigma := \{c \in S(V,\Sigma) \mid \operatorname{Supp}(c) = \sigma\}$$

carries the subspace topology from $[0,1]^V$.

---

### The candidate homeomorphism

Define

$$\varphi : S_\sigma \longrightarrow \Delta^{\circ}_{n-1}, \qquad \varphi(c) = \big(c(v_1),\, c(v_2),\, \dots,\, c(v_n)\big).$$

This is well-defined: for $c \in S_\sigma$, we have $\operatorname{Supp}(c) = \sigma$, so $c(v_i) \neq 0$, i.e. $c(v_i) > 0$ (since $c$ takes values in $[0,1]$), and $\sum_{v \in V} c(v) = 1$ with $c(v) = 0$ for $v \notin \sigma$ gives $\sum_{i=1}^{n} c(v_i) = 1$. Hence $\varphi(c) \in \Delta^{\circ}_{n-1}$.

Define the inverse

$$\psi : \Delta^{\circ}_{n-1} \longrightarrow S_\sigma, \qquad \psi(x_1,\dots,x_n)(v) = \begin{cases} x_i & \text{if } v = v_i \in \sigma, \\ 0 & \text{if } v \notin \sigma. \end{cases}$$

This is well-defined: $\psi(x)$ takes values in $[0,1]$, has $\operatorname{Supp}(\psi(x)) = \sigma$ (since every $x_i > 0$), and $\sum_{v} \psi(x)(v) = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i = 1$, so $\psi(x) \in S_\sigma$.

Clearly $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are mutual inverses, so $\varphi$ is a bijection.

---

### Continuity of $\varphi$

The map $\varphi$ is the restriction to $S_\sigma$ of the coordinate projection

$$[0,1]^V \xrightarrow{\;\pi_\sigma\;} [0,1]^\sigma \cong [0,1]^n \xrightarrow{\;\text{incl}\;} \mathbb{R}^n,$$

where $\pi_\sigma$ selects the coordinates indexed by $\sigma$. Coordinate projections are continuous in the product topology, and the inclusion $[0,1]^n \hookrightarrow \mathbb{R}^n$ is continuous. Hence $\varphi$ is continuous.

---

### Continuity of $\psi$

A map into a product space $[0,1]^V$ is continuous if and only if every coordinate composition $\pi_v \circ \psi : \Delta^{\circ}_{n-1} \to [0,1]$ is continuous (universal property of the product topology). For each $v \in V$:

- If $v = v_i \in \sigma$, then $\pi_v \circ \psi$ is the projection $(x_1,\dots,x_n) \mapsto x_i$, which is continuous.
- If $v \notin \sigma$, then $\pi_v \circ \psi$ is the constant zero map, which is continuous.

Therefore $\psi : \Delta^{\circ}_{n-1} \to [0,1]^V$ is continuous. Since its image lies in $S_\sigma$, it is continuous as a map $\Delta^{\circ}_{n-1} \to S_\sigma$.

---

### Conclusion

$\varphi : S_\sigma \to \Delta^{\circ}_{n-1}$ is a continuous bijection with continuous inverse $\psi$. Hence $\varphi$ is a homeomorphism between

$$\{c \in S(V,\Sigma) \mid \operatorname{Supp}(c) = \sigma\} \quad\text{and}\quad \Delta^{\circ}_{|\sigma|-1},$$

an open simplex of dimension $|\sigma| - 1$, one less than the number of vertices in $\sigma$. $\blacksquare$
